first.rationale: The two metrics actually degrading are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), so the highest-leverage single slot is the funnel step upstream of both. memory_31 and memory_86 both point at onboarding/signup friction, and memory_91 (activation messaging) is a complementary but downstream lever that works better once completion recovers. I am deliberately NOT leading with promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 is compressed to 'strong acquisition and revenue lift,' which is exactly the shape of claim that loses its caveats in consolidation \u2014 acquisition lift from discounting routinely coexists with lower-LTV cohorts, margin erosion, and anchoring effects that surface after the measurement window. Matching a price attack also concedes the competitor's chosen battlefield and is hard to reverse. Hence verification spend: (1) memory_73, to see whether the archived record measured retained/qualified revenue or only signups and top-line, since that single fact determines whether pricing is a trap; (2) memory_86, because it is the memory I intend to act on \u2014 I want to confirm the original record shows shortened onboarding lifting durable adoption rather than just completion rate, and that field-cutting did not degrade lead qualification or routing data (which would quietly harm the enterprise path in memory_44). Both inherited onboarding results are old (day 12, day 52) and predate the current competitive mix, so their effect sizes are directional, not guaranteed \u2014 I treat them as hypotheses to re-test, not settled facts. Running at standard experiment scale with holdout, instrumented on activation and week-4 retained revenue rather than completion alone; if verification shows memory_86's lift was completion-only cosmetics, I would fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91) rather than to discounting.

final.rationale: Verification resolved both questions decisively. exp_86 held up on the durable metric, not just the cosmetic one: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. That is a real improvement in delivered value, and it is aimed squarely at the two metrics actually degrading this quarter (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%). exp_73 was the trap I suspected: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% looked strong in the consolidated memory, but the source record shows 30-day retention -12% and an explicit conclusion NOT to generalize targeted discounting as sustainable growth. The consolidation to memory_73 had stripped the retention loss and the warning entirely, leaving a claim that would have led straight into the competitor's chosen battlefield with a cohort that does not survive first renewal. Against the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, discounting is disqualified on its own evidence, and I am flagging memory_73 as actively misleading in its current compressed form so the next session does not re-inherit the sanitized version. Referral (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) address neither degrading metric this week; activation_messaging (memory_91) is the right second move but works better downstream of a recovered completion rate, so it is my fallback and likely next slot. Running at standard scale with a holdout, instrumented on activation and week-4 retained revenue rather than completion alone. Residual uncertainty: exp_86 is day-52 evidence predating the current competitive mix, so I treat the +13%/+3% as directional rather than a promised effect size, and I will watch that cutting signup fields does not degrade lead-qualification data feeding the enterprise demo path. Fixing our own funnel is also the reversible move; a price cut anchors expectations and is hard to walk back.
